claim: The poles of the mitotic spindle contain one old and one young centrosome.
source: The poles of the mitotic spindle contain one old and one young centrosome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about mitotic spindles.

claim: In asymmetric stem cell divisions, the age of centrosomes affects their behaviour and their probability to remain in the stem cell.
source: In asymmetric stem cell divisions, the age of centrosomes affects their behaviour and their probability to remain in the stem cell.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: In symmetric divisions, old and young centrosomes are thought to behave equally.
source: In contrast, in symmetric divisions, old and young centrosomes are thought to behave equally.
evidence: This is stated as a prevailing hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Kinetochore–microtubules associated to old centrosomes are more stable than those associated to young centrosomes in symmetrically dividing human cells.
source: In this study, we show in symmetrically dividing human cells that kinetochore–microtubules associated to old centrosomes are more stable than those associated to young centrosomes
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The difference in kinetochore-microtubule stability favours the accumulation of premature end-on attachments that delay the alignment of polar chromosomes at old centrosomes.
source: kinetochore–microtubules associated to old centrosomes are more stable than those associated to young centrosomes, and that this difference favours the accumulation of premature end-on attachments that delay the alignment of polar chromosomes at old centrosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3C,D showing higher percentages of end-on attachments at old centrosomes.

claim: The differential microtubule stability depends on cenexin, a protein enriched on old centrosomes.
source: This differential microtubule stability depends on cenexin, a protein enriched on old centrosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing that cenexin depletion abolishes the bias in chromosome alignment and end-on attachments (Figure 3I,J,D).

claim: The differential microtubule stability persists throughout mitosis.
source: It persists throughout mitosis, biasing chromosome segregation in anaphase
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing biased segregation of non-disjoint chromosomes in anaphase (Figure 4).

claim: Daughter cells with old centrosomes retain non-disjoint chromosomes 85% of the time.
source: biasing chromosome segregation in anaphase by causing daughter cells with old centrosomes to retain non-disjoint chromosomes 85% of the time.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Table 2 showing 18 out of 21 non-disjoint chromosomes co-segregated with old centrosomes (85.7%).

claim: Centrosome age imposes via cenexin a functional asymmetry on all mitotic spindles.
source: We conclude that centrosome age imposes via cenexin a functional asymmetry on all mitotic spindles.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Every centrosome is duplicated once during the cell cycle, resulting in the presence of an old and young centrosome at mitotic onset.
source: The bipolar spindle has a symmetric appearance; nevertheless it contains two centrosomes of different ages, as every centrosome is duplicated once during the cell cycle, resulting in the presence of an old and young centrosome at mitotic onset (Nigg and Stearns, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In asymmetric stem cell divisions centrosome age differentially affects their capacity to nucleate microtubules and their positioning with respect to the polarity and cell division axis.
source: In asymmetric stem cell divisions centrosome age differentially affects their capacity to nucleate microtubules and their positioning with respect to the polarity and cell division axis (Yamashita et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2009; Januschke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Stem cells stereotypically inherit the centrosome which nucleates more microtubules, which in most cases is the old centrosome.
source: Stem cells stereotypically inherit the centrosome, which nucleates more microtubules, which in most cases is the old centrosome (except in fly neuroblast divisions, where stem cells retain the young active centrosome; Januschke et al., 2011, Conduit and Raff, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In fly neuroblast divisions, stem cells retain the young active centrosome.
source: except in fly neuroblast divisions, where stem cells retain the young active centrosome; Januschke et al., 2011, Conduit and Raff, 2010
evidence: This is stated as an exception in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Old centrosomes co-segregate with the ciliary membrane in stem cell divisions, allowing daughter stem cells to form a primary cilium earlier than the differentiating daughter cells.
source: Old centrosomes also co-segregate with the ciliary membrane in stem cell divisions, allowing daughter stem cells to form a primary cilium earlier than the differentiating daughter cells (Paridaen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The old and young centrosomes can be differentiated at the ultra-structural level in symmetric divisions.
source: In symmetric divisions, the old and young centrosomes can be differentiated at the ultra-structural level, and in terms of their microtubule-anchoring capacity during interphase (Rieder and Borisy, 1982; Piel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The old and young centrosomes can be differentiated in terms of their microtubule-anchoring capacity during interphase.
source: In symmetric divisions, the old and young centrosomes can be differentiated at the ultra-structural level, and in terms of their microtubule-anchoring capacity during interphase (Rieder and Borisy, 1982; Piel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The oldest centriole within the old centrosome contains distal and subdistal appendages.
source: The oldest centriole within the old centrosome contains distal and subdistal appendages
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about centrosome structure.

claim: Distal appendages are necessary for centrioles to become basal bodies that can contact the plasma membrane.
source: the first are necessary for centrioles to become basal bodies that can contact the plasma membrane (Graser et al., 2007; Hoyer-Fender, 2010)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Subdistal appendages are involved in the organization of the interphase microtubule network, due to the presence of ninein, a key microtubule-anchoring protein.
source: while the latter are involved in the organization of the interphase microtubule network, due to the presence of ninein, a key microtubule-anchoring protein (Mogensen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Both distal and subdistal appendage structures require the presence of cenexin.
source: Both structures require the presence of cenexin, the oldest known marker for old centrosomes and appendages (Lange and Gull, 1995; Ishikawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Cenexin is the oldest known marker for old centrosomes and appendages.
source: cenexin, the oldest known marker for old centrosomes and appendages (Lange and Gull, 1995; Ishikawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: All structural differences between old and young centrosomes disappear progressively as cells enter mitosis.
source: Importantly, all these structural differences disappear progressively as cells enter mitosis
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: It is assumed that the old and the young centrosomes behave indistinguishably in symmetrically dividing cells, resulting in a symmetric bipolar spindle.
source: therefore, it is assumed that the old and the young centrosomes behave indistinguishably in symmetrically dividing cells, resulting in a symmetric bipolar spindle.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a prevailing assumption.

claim: The hypothesis that old and young centrosomes behave indistinguishably in symmetrically dividing cells has never been directly tested at the functional level.
source: This hypothesis has, however, never been directly tested at the functional level.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction to establish the novelty of the study.

claim: 61.23% of unaligned chromosomes were in the vicinity of old centrosomes in untreated HeLa-eGFP-centrin1 cells.
source: We found that 61.23% of the unaligned chromosomes were in the vicinity of old centrosomes in Hela-eGFP-centrin1 cells as opposed to 50% expected for an unbiased distribution
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: Treatment with 10 ng/ml nocodazole moderately stabilizes microtubules.
source: we also treated cells with 10 ng/ml nocodazole, a condition that moderately stabilizes microtubules (Vasquez et al., 1997)
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Treatment with 10 ng/ml nocodazole delays chromosome alignment, leading to 3–6 unaligned chromosomes per cell.
source: and that delays chromosome alignment, leading to 3–6 unaligned chromosomes per cell (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figure 1C.

claim: 63.9% of unaligned chromosomes were preferentially found in the vicinity of old centrosomes in HeLa eGFP-centrin1 cells treated with 10 ng/ml nocodazole.
source: Unaligned chromosomes were again preferentially found in the vicinity of the old centrosomes in HeLa eGFP-centrin1 (63.9%)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: 71.8% of unaligned chromosomes were preferentially found in the vicinity of old centrosomes in hTert-RPE1-eGFP-centrin1 cells treated with 10 ng/ml nocodazole.
source: and hTert-RPE1-eGFP-centrin1 cells (71.8%)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: 67.8% of unaligned chromosomes were found in the vicinity of old centrosomes in wild-type nocodazole-treated hTert-RPE1 cells stained with cenexin.
source: We found the same bias (67.8%) in wild-type nocodazole-treated hTert-RPE1 cells stained with cenexin, excluding any effect due to eGFP-centrin1 expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: There is no difference in the distances between kinetochores and old and young centrosomes at mitotic onset.
source: To test whether at mitotic onset old centrosomes capture kinetochores faster because they are closer, we compared the distances between kinetochores and old and young centrosomes at mitotic onset, but found no difference (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: 74.4% of unaligned chromosomes were adjacent to old centrosomes after monastrol washout in hTert-RPE1 cells.
source: A monastrol washout led to bipolar spindles with few unaligned chromosomes, 74.4% of which were adjacent to old centrosomes, indicating that the bias is independent of the initial centrosome position (Figure 2B,C; and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2B,C and Table 1.

claim: The bias in chromosome alignment is independent of the initial centrosome position.
source: 74.4% of which were adjacent to old centrosomes, indicating that the bias is independent of the initial centrosome position
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the monastrol washout experiment.

claim: 62.6% of unaligned chromosomes were adjacent to old centrosomes after nocodazole washout.
source: To test whether old centrosomes capture more kinetochores because they mature earlier, we treated cells with high doses of nocodazole (1 μg/ml), allowing them to enter mitosis without microtubules and to fully mature the two centrosomes (Khodjakov and Rieder, 1999), before washing out nocodazole for 1 hr: 62.6% of the unaligned chromosomes were adjacent to old centrosomes
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2B,C and Table 1.

claim: The alignment bias reflects a permanent difference between the centrosomes that is independent of the initial conditions at mitotic onset.
source: indicating that the alignment bias reflects a permanent difference between the centrosomes that is independent of the initial conditions at mitotic onset (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the nocodazole washout experiment.

claim: The bias in chromosome alignment does not require low nocodazole concentrations.
source: The two washout experiments also confirmed that this bias does not require low nocodazole concentrations, since in both cases, cells were released in nocodazole-free medium.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the washout experiments.

claim: A microtubule re-nucleation assay revealed no difference in microtubule nucleation capacity between the two centrosomes in HeLa and RPE1 cells.
source: However, a microtubule re-nucleation assay revealed no difference in microtubule nucleation capacity between the two centrosomes in HeLa and RPE1 cells (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Partial CENP-E inhibition abolished the bias in the distribution of unaligned chromosomes in the absence or presence of 10 ng/ml nocodazole.
source: Partial CENP-E inhibition, yielding few polar chromosomes, abolished the bias in the distribution of unaligned chromosomes in the absence or presence of 10 ng/ml nocodazole, (Figure 2F,G, 49.87% and 52.29% respectively)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2F,G and Table 1.

claim: The bias in chromosome alignment depends on CENP-E.
source: indicating that the bias depends on CENP-E, and that chromosome alignment itself is biased by centrosome age.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the CENP-E inhibition experiment.

claim: The levels of CENP-E on unaligned chromosomes associated to old or young centrosomes were equal.
source: The CENP-E-dependent alignment bias could be due to an asymmetric abundance of CENP-E; however, the levels of CENP-E on unaligned chromosomes associated to old or young centrosomes were equal (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: At old centrosomes nearly three times more individual kinetochores had end-on attachments (13.0% vs 4.7% at the young centrosome, p = 0.003 in paired t-test).
source: At old centrosomes nearly three times more individual kinetochores had end-on attachments (13.0% vs 4.7% at the young centrosome, p = 0.003 in paired t-test)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Fewer kinetochores had lateral attachments at old centrosomes (83.6% vs 89.1% at the young centrosomes; p = 0.0007 in paired t-test).
source: and fewer lateral attachments (83.6% vs 89.1% at the young centrosomes; p = 0.0007 in paired t-test; overall p = 0.0024 in 2way-ANOVA-test; Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Tubulin acetylation preferentially accumulates on stable microtubules.
source: To confirm this result, we quantified the levels of tubulin acetylation on individual kinetochore–fibres of sister-kinetochore pairs aligned on the metaphase plate, as tubulin acetylation preferentially accumulates on stable microtubules (Webster and Borisy, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation to support the claim.

claim: There are higher levels of acetylation on kinetochore–microtubules associated with old centrosomes (median difference of 22% in tubulin acetylation at the plus ends of microtubules attached to sister-kinetochores vs 2% in CREST levels between sister-kinetochores, p < 0.0001 in Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test).
source: This analysis revealed higher level of acetylation on kinetochore–microtubules associated with old centrosomes (median difference of 22% in tubulin acetylation at the plus ends of microtubules attached to sister-kinetochores vs 2% in CREST levels between sister-kinetochores, p < 0.0001 in Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test; Figure 3E,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3E,F.

claim: There is no difference in the levels of detyrosinated tubulin between kinetochore-microtubules associated with old and young centrosomes (median difference of 0.3%).
source: In contrast, when we measured the levels of detyrosinated tubulin, a modification that has been linked to preferential CENP-E motor activity (Barisic et al., 2015), we found no difference (median difference of 0.3%; Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: Kinetochores oriented towards young centrosomes were significantly more likely to have lost their attachment after Ca2+ treatment than those oriented towards the old centrosome (56.8% vs 43.2%; p = 0.014 in paired t-test).
source: a detailed analysis of kinetochore–microtubule attachments of aligned sister-kinetochores revealed that kinetochores oriented towards young centrosomes were significantly more likely to have lost their attachment, than those oriented towards the old centrosome (56.8% vs 43.2%; p = 0.014 in paired t-test; Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3G,H.

claim: The kinetochore–microtubules emanating from old centrosomes are more stable.
source: Together, these data indicated that the kinetochore–microtubules emanating from old centrosomes are more stable.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: Depletion of Dsn1 or Nnf1 abolished the bias in alignment and equalized the number of end-on attached unaligned kinetochores.
source: To test if the difference in kinetochore–microtubule stability is at the origin of the alignment bias, we depleted the kinetochore proteins Dsn1 or Nnf1 (both Mis12 complex), or treated the cells with a low dose of taxol (5 nM). These conditions strongly destabilize kinetochore–microtubules (Dsn1 and Nnf1 depletion; (Kline et al., 2006), or hyperstabilize kinetochore–microtubules (taxol; Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Either treatment abolished the bias in alignment and equalized the number of end-on attached unaligned kinetochores (Figure 3D,I,J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3D,I,J.

claim: Treatment with 5 nM taxol abolished the bias in alignment and equalized the number of end-on attached unaligned kinetochores.
source: To test if the difference in kinetochore–microtubule stability is at the origin of the alignment bias, we depleted the kinetochore proteins Dsn1 or Nnf1 (both Mis12 complex), or treated the cells with a low dose of taxol (5 nM). These conditions strongly destabilize kinetochore–microtubules (Dsn1 and Nnf1 depletion; (Kline et al., 2006), or hyperstabilize kinetochore–microtubules (taxol; Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Either treatment abolished the bias in alignment and equalized the number of end-on attached unaligned kinetochores (Figure 3D,I,J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3D,I,J.

claim: Knock-down of MCAK did not change the bias in chromosome alignment.
source: In contrast, knock-down of the Mitotic Centromere-Associated Kinesin (MCAK), a microtubule depolymerase that is required for destabilization of erroneous kinetochore–microtubule attachments (Knowlton et al., 2006), whose depletion leads to mild microtubule stabilization in metaphase, but not in prometaphase ((Bakhoum et al., 2009) and Figure 3—figure supplement 3), did not change the bias in chromosome alignment (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3I,J.

claim: The difference in kinetochore–microtubule stability biases chromosome alignment.
source: We conclude that the difference in kinetochore–microtubule stability biases chromosome alignment.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: There is a modest increase of active Aurora-A on old centrosomes in HeLa cells.
source: While Plk1 was symmetrically distributed, we found a modest increase of active Aurora-A on old centrosomes in HeLa cells (Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3K.

claim: The difference in active Aurora-A on old centrosomes is not present in RPE1 cells.
source: This difference was, however, not present in RPE1 cells (Figure 3K)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3K.

claim: Inhibition of Aurora-A or Plk1 did not abolish the bias in chromosome alignment.
source: moreover inhibition of Aurora-A or Plk1 did not abolish the bias in chromosome alignment, indicating that it does not depend on these two kinases (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3L.

claim: The bias in chromosome alignment does not depend on Aurora-A or Plk1.
source: indicating that it does not depend on these two kinases
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the kinase inhibition experiments.

claim: Ninein depletion had no effect on chromosome alignment.
source: While ninein depletion had no effect on chromosome alignment, cenexin depletion randomized the distribution of unaligned chromosomes (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3I,J.

claim: Cenexin depletion randomized the distribution of unaligned chromosomes.
source: cenexin depletion randomized the distribution of unaligned chromosomes (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3I,J.

claim: Cenexin depletion equalized the percentage of end-on attached kinetochores at unaligned chromosomes.
source: Furthermore, it also equalized the percentage of end-on attached kinetochores at unaligned chromosomes, indicating that cenexin affects kinetochore–microtubule stability (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: Cenexin affects kinetochore–microtubule stability.
source: indicating that cenexin affects kinetochore–microtubule stability
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the cenexin depletion experiment.

claim: Old centrosomes stabilize kinetochore–microtubules in a cenexin-dependent manner.
source: We conclude that old centrosomes stabilize kinetochore–microtubules in a cenexin-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: In roughly 2–5% of anaphases, there was the presence of two lagging kinetochores that moved in synchrony between the two daughter DNA masses, but were separated by several microns, suggesting a sister-kinetochore pair on a non-disjoint chromosome.
source: However, in addition in roughly 2–5% of anaphases, we observed the presence of two lagging kinetochores that moved in synchrony between the two daughter DNA masses, but were separated by several microns, suggesting a sister-kinetochore pair on a non-disjoint chromosome (Figure 4A and Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4A and Video 1.

claim: Such kinetochore pairs were invariably connected by a DNA thread.
source: This assumption was confirmed by high-resolution immunofluorescence imaging, as such kinetochore pairs were invariably connected by a DNA thread (see representative images in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: 18 out of the 21 analyzed kinetochore pairs co-segregated with the old centrosome.
source: In those instances where both sister-kinetochores segregated to the same daughter cell, we found a strong bias in chromosome mis-segregation as 18 out of the 21 analyzed kinetochore pairs co-segregated with the old centrosome (Figure 4C; Video 1; number of experiments, cells and statistical tests for all chromosome mis-segregation events are in Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4C and Table 2.

claim: Treatment with Nnf1 siRNA abolished the bias in chromosome mis-segregation.
source: To test this hypothesis, we treated cells with Nnf1 and Cenexin siRNAs, which had abolished the bias in chromosome alignment and the asymmetry in the percentage of end-on attached kinetochores. In both cases, the bias in chromosome mis-segregation was abolished (Figure 4C; Video 2 and 3)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4C and Table 2.

claim: Treatment with Cenexin siRNA abolished the bias in chromosome mis-segregation.
source: To test this hypothesis, we treated cells with Nnf1 and Cenexin siRNAs, which had abolished the bias in chromosome alignment and the asymmetry in the percentage of end-on attached kinetochores. In both cases, the bias in chromosome mis-segregation was abolished (Figure 4C; Video 2 and 3)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4C and Table 2.

claim: When MCAK was depleted, chromosome mis-segregation was still biased.
source: in contrast when we depleted MCAK, which did not abolish the bias in chromosome alignment, chromosome mis-segregation was still biased (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4C and Table 2.

claim: The difference in the stability of kinetochore–microtubules bound to the old or the young centrosome persists in anaphase.
source: We conclude that the difference in the stability of kinetochore–microtubules bound to the old or the young centrosome persists in anaphase, and that this difference causes non-disjoint chromosomes to co-segregate with old centrosomes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: The difference in kinetochore-microtubule stability causes non-disjoint chromosomes to co-segregate with old centrosomes.
source: We conclude that the difference in the stability of kinetochore–microtubules bound to the old or the young centrosome persists in anaphase, and that this difference causes non-disjoint chromosomes to co-segregate with old centrosomes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Even in symmetrically dividing cells the two half-spindles behave in an asymmetric manner.
source: Our results demonstrate that even in symmetrically dividing cells the two half-spindles behave in an asymmetric manner, and that centrosome age imposes a functional asymmetry on all mitotic spindles (see model Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the discussion.

claim: The asymmetry in half-spindle behavior reflects a differential stability of kinetochore–microtubules that depends on the presence of cenexin at old centrosomes.
source: We find that this asymmetry reflects a differential stability of kinetochore–microtubules that depends on the presence of cenexin at old centrosomes, indicating that its presence influences the relative stability of kinetochore–microtubules.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the discussion.

claim: Knock-out of cenexin does not impair mitotic progression.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that knock-out of cenexin does not impair mitotic progression; it contributes, however, to the stability of the centrosome-bound microtubules during interphase, consistent with our findings that cenexin affects mitotic microtubules (Ishikawa et al., 2005; Tateishi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Cenexin contributes to the stability of the centrosome-bound microtubules during interphase.
source: it contributes, however, to the stability of the centrosome-bound microtubules during interphase, consistent with our findings that cenexin affects mitotic microtubules (Ishikawa et al., 2005; Tateishi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Cenexin is required for the formation of distal and sub-distal appendages on the oldest centriole.
source: It is required for the formation of distal and sub-distal appendages on the oldest centriole, two structures that are essential for the formation of basal bodies during ciliogenesis (Ishikawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Distal and sub-distal appendages are essential for the formation of basal bodies during ciliogenesis.
source: two structures that are essential for the formation of basal bodies during ciliogenesis (Ishikawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The asymmetry in kinetochore–microtubule stability persists throughout mitosis and directs the fate of non-disjoint chromosomes, which co-segregate mostly with the old centrosome.
source: The asymmetry in kinetochore–microtubule stability persists throughout mitosis and directs the fate of non-disjoint chromosomes, which co-segregate mostly with the old centrosome.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the discussion.

claim: It is unclear whether the asymmetry in kinetochore-microtubule stability serves a direct purpose during mitosis, or if it is a consequence of a centrosome asymmetry that is required for a non-mitotic function.
source: At present it is unclear whether this asymmetry serves a direct purpose during mitosis, or if it a consequence of a centrosome asymmetry that is required for a non-mitotic function, but which cells have to deal with during each cell division.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the discussion.

claim: Possible non-mitotic purposes of centrosome asymmetry include the necessity to only have one centriole capable of generating the basal body of a cilium.
source: Possible non-mitotic purposes of this asymmetry include the necessity to only have one centriole capable of generating the basal body of a cilium, or the requirement to only have one centriole capable of anchoring interphase microtubules (Piel et al., 2000; Nigg and Raff, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the discussion with citations.

claim: Possible non-mitotic purposes of centrosome asymmetry include the requirement to only have one centriole capable of anchoring interphase microtubules.
source: Possible non-mitotic purposes of this asymmetry include the necessity to only have one centriole capable of generating the basal body of a cilium, or the requirement to only have one centriole capable of anchoring interphase microtubules (Piel et al., 2000; Nigg and Raff, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the discussion with citations.

claim: A possible mitotic function for an asymmetric behaviour of centrosomes is that it might protect stem cells that inherit the old centrosome, from losing non-disjoint chromosomes.
source: A possible mitotic function for an asymmetric behaviour of centrosomes is that it might protect stem cells that inherit the old centrosome, from losing non-disjoint chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the discussion.

claim: Haplo-insufficiency is much more frequent than triplo-lethality at the level of single genes in animal cells.
source: This would provide a selective advantage, as haplo-insufficiency is much more frequent than triplo-lethality at the level of single genes in animal cells (Lindsley et al., 1972; Torres et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: The asymmetric distribution of non-disjoint chromosomes might favour the rapid acquisition of new traits by co-occurrence of chromosome gains in cancer-stem cells.
source: We speculate that the asymmetric distribution of non-disjoint chromosomes might, however, also favour the rapid acquisition of new traits by co-occurrence of chromosome gains in cancer-stem cells.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the discussion.

claim: The analysis of large human cancer samples reveals that whole chromosome gains (or losses) co-occur at much higher frequencies than combined chromosome gains and losses.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis we note that the analysis of large human cancer samples reveals that whole chromosome gains (or losses) co-occur at much higher frequencies than combined chromosome gains and losses (Ozery-Flato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The co-occurrence of whole chromosome gains or losses was thought to be the result of an evolutionary pressure.
source: This phenomenon was so far thought to be the result of an evolutionary pressure
